transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-11-14 16:00 UTC / Duration: 1:02 / RecordID: ff-20281114-orion-001
Attendees: Morgan B (Redwood AE), Sahil R (Redwood SE), Clara N (Redwood SE), Aisha K (Orion VP Product), Daniel W (Lead ML Eng), Renee P (Security)

Auto-generated summary: Quick intro to Redwood's JSON mode and demo of structured actions with guardrails. Customer concerned about data residency and safe tool execution.

[00:00] Morgan (Redwood): All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Morgan from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Sahil and Clara from our engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Aisha (Orion): Good, thanks. Excited to see the JSON mode flow — we've been reading the docs.
[00:12] Daniel (Orion): Yeah, we want to make sure the assistant can call our internal services without leaking PII — that's the main ask.
[00:19] Morgan: Totally, that's what we'll focus on. Quick agenda: run through JSON/schema enforcement, show tool/function calling with safe fallbacks, then jump into the Console and Optimize suggestions for cost/latency.
[00:30] Renee: Also, offline we'll need SOC2 and network diagrams.
[00:33] Morgan: Absolutely, we'll share those.
[00:36] Sahil (Redwood): I'll kick off with the runtime behavior — high level — then demo a live flow. Note: apologies if the transcript slurs some acronyms, sometimes V P C gets written weird.

[03:05] Sahil: Okay, so JSON mode is basically contracts-first. You give the model a schema for the output shape — typed fields, enums, validation rules — and the runtime enforces that the model either returns valid JSON or we run the extractor and can auto-correct with retries. So for tool calling, we also tie the response to an action schema. That lets you map to internal APIs safely.
[03:42] Daniel: So if the model suggests a tool call like get_customer_profile, how do we prevent it from calling arbitrary endpoints?
[03:50] Sahil: Good question. Two layers: first, the schema restricts which actions are valid — you ship a finite action set to the runtime. Second, the routing layer maps action names to whitelisted endpoints per deployment — Hosted vs Dedicated and in Private you control the mappings entirely.
[04:12] Aisha: And what about parameters? We need to avoid sensitive fields being sent.
[04:18] Sahil: We support parameter-level sanitization and tokenization configs. We also have prefix-level KV caching so the assistant can reuse context without shipping raw PII to the call if you opt into masked caching. There's also an allowlist per action for which attributes can be forwarded.
[04:38] Renee: Sounds good. For our compliance team we need KMS integration and audit logs for every call. Is that baked in?
[04:45] Clara: Yes — in Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and generate per-request audit events. Hosted has configurable retention and export hooks; Dedicated adds the extra audit retention and role-based access controls.
[05:00] Renee: Great. Can you show us a concrete example?

[06:10] Sahil: Demo time. I'm going to switch to the Console. I'm loading a sample assistant that Orion can use for support routing. The schema here is small: action.name enum {lookup_account, escalate_to_human, fetch_order}, payload with masked fields like account_id (string) and reason (enum).
[06:34] [screen share glitches briefly]
[06:40] Sahil: Sorry screen share got a hiccup. All right, here's a prompt: "Customer says: 'my delivery is late, order 234-XY'". The model returns an action: {"action":"fetch_order","payload":{"order_ref":"234-XY"}} and the runtime validates against the schema.
[07:02] Daniel: If the model instead returns free text, does Redwood attempt to coerce it to JSON?
[07:08] Sahil: Yes, the extractor layer tries a deterministic parse and if it fails we have a retry policy. You can tune retry depth and whether to fall back to a human escalation action.
[07:20] Morgan: Important for high-throughput flows: you can enable strict JSON mode which will reject non-conforming output and route to a safe fallback. That avoids downstream side effects.
[07:31] Aisha: What's the latency impact of strict mode? We have sub-300ms SLO for some paths.
[07:36] Sahil: It depends — if you do additional retries that adds a small tail. Typical single-shot strict validation adds ~5-12ms. Retries add token latency proportional to context length. But we also have batching options in Redwood Optimize that can amortize cost for async routes.
[08:00] Tom (Orion): Can you talk more about Optimize? We need guidance on quantization and batching for our heavy embedding workload.
[08:06] Clara: Sure. Optimize looks at your request distribution, suggests model variants (quantized, FP16), batching parameters, and cache TTLs. For embeddings-heavy jobs, we often recommend larger batch sizes and quantized models to save tokens while keeping similarity fidelity. We can run a cost projection for Hosted vs Dedicated.
[08:30] Renee: For Dedicated, how isolated is it? Are there shared nodes?
[08:35] Sahil: Dedicated means reserved GPU pools for your account. No noisy neighbor in the same instance; we do strict tenancy at the allocation level. For Private on-prem or VPC, you control the networking and compute — Redwood's control plane can be separated or a light local control plane.
[08:51] Daniel: If we want to test, what's a minimal pilot look like?
[08:56] Morgan: Usually a two-week pilot: sample traffic replay to our staging, a perf benchmark, and a small schema-first assistant that calls one or two internal endpoints. We'll include a sandbox config for the routing mappings.
[09:10] Renee: Are there any common pitfalls when mapping actions to internal microservices?
[09:15] Sahil: Yes — make sure your action granularity is coarse enough; avoid allowing free-form arbitrary SQL or arbitrary url fields. Use strongly typed payloads. Also, set fallback policies: rate-limited tool retries, and a human escalation if validation repeatedly fails.
[09:28] Aisha: Can the runtime do partial responses? For example, return structured data and then stream a human-readable summary?
[09:34] Sahil: We support streaming structured chunks — the runtime can emit partial typed fragments and concurrently stream a generation for user-facing text. That's useful for long-running tasks.
[09:45] Morgan: Quick note: we also have function-call style semantics in the API, but our Console exposes a JSON-mode playground that lets you define action schemas and test tool invocation end-to-end.

[12:12] [15:00] Demo: Tool routing map. Sahil shows mapping UI where action name maps to URL and auth method. There's an option to set "masking policy" per param.
[15:45] Daniel: In their UI I see an option for "allow-token-substitution" — is that safe?
[15:50] Sahil: It's safe if you restrict which roles can create that mapping and enable KMS. If misconfigured it could leak sensitive data so we recommend review by security owners.
[16:05] Renee: Can I get a CSV of every action call for audit?
[16:09] Clara: Yes, audit export and stream to SIEM is available, we can push logs to your log pipeline via secure transfer.

[22:20] Aisha: We also run models in-house — curious about hybrid routing: use our private for PII queries and fallback to hosted for generic chit-chat. How would that work?
[22:31] Sahil: Smart routing supports policies: route-by-intent, route-by-cost, route-by-region. For example, tag intents that touch PII and route to Private deployment; non-sensitive go to Hosted. You can also do traffic split.
[22:48] Daniel: What's the integration burden for our infra team? We use Terraform and internal CI CI — can we automate the mappings?
[22:56] Morgan: Yes, we have an API and Terraform provider for configs — developers can check in action definitions and the console picks them up.

[30:00] [30:05] Live failure simulation: Sahil shows malformed model output -> runtime applies extractor attempt -> still invalid -> runtime triggers fallback action "escalate_to_human". Transcript shows a few garbled tokens when the extractor ran (the transcription engine shows "K V cash" instead of KV cache).
[30:25] Aisha: Good to see the escalation. How is human-in-the-loop latency typically?
[30:29] Sahil: Depends on your workflow. If your CS team uses our integrations (Slack, Zendesk), it's near realtime; for manual review queues expect minutes.

[36:00] Morgan: Let's talk TCO briefly. For an assistant hitting ~2M tokens/day with some embedding ops, Dedicated tends to be cheaper if sustained load, Hosted is faster to iterate. Optimize can cut 20-40% by batching/caching and model substitution.
[36:20] Daniel: Any numbers you can share now?
[36:23] Morgan: We'll include a TCO spreadsheet in the follow-up, but as a ballpark, a dedicated pool with 4x A100 equivalent for steady inference is often ~X per month compared to Hosted variable usage — we'll spell out assumptions in the proposal.

[44:10] Renee: Security checklist — SSO, RBAC, customer KMS, network egress controls, audit retention. Do you have a standard pack?
[44:18] Clara: Yes, we have a security pack with SOC2, ISO artifacts, and sample network diagrams. We'll send over the pack and schedule a technical security review.

[50:00] Morgan: Any remaining technical questions?
[50:05] Tom: Can you do a short runbook for a deploy rollback if a model starts hallucinating actions?
[50:10] Sahil: Yes — best practice: enforce schema-level rejection, enable canary traffic split, and set automatic fallback to a conservative model or human triage. We'll prototype a runbook for you.

[58:30] Morgan: OK, recap and next steps — we will: send pilot proposal, share SOC2 + network docs, provide benchmark harness, and schedule a perf run in your staging. Do we have agreement on that timeline?
[58:44] Aisha: That works. We'll aim to review by 11/19 and confirm the pilot start.
[58:50] Daniel: I'll collect the sample prompts and traffic profile.
[58:55] Renee: I'll send security questions this week.
[59:05] Morgan: Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials.

[60:30] End of recording.
